title: "About"

## Introduction

The exchange rate is one of the most important prices in an economy. It acts as an automatic stabiliser and affects all aspects of finance, from trade to foreign flows. Macro traders, central bankers and other finance professionals are therefore interested in the de facto exchange rate decisions of central banks, which can differ from the regime a country announces [@calvo2002fear; @ilzetzki2022rethinking].

@sharma2026 implement the methodology developed in @zeileis2010testing for 41 emerging market economies, revealing the de facto behaviour of central banks in FX markets. This website operationalises that work and keeps it up to date.

## Methodology

Following @zeileis2010testing, the de facto regime of a currency is inferred by regressing its returns on the returns of a basket of major currencies, with all rates measured against a neutral numeraire currency, as in @frankel1994yen. The coefficients are the basket weights: a weight on the US dollar close to one with a high $R^2$ points to a dollar peg, while small weights and a low $R^2$ point to a float.

The weights are allowed to change over time. Structural break dates are estimated with the multiple-break framework of @bai1998estimating, as implemented in the `fxregime` R package, and the number of breaks is chosen by the BIC. Each stretch between two breaks is a regime, and for each regime the site reports the estimated weights, the $R^2$ and the residual variance.

Default settings used on this website:

- weekly exchange rate returns, from the bilateral exchange rates published by the BIS [@bisdata];
- numeraire: New Zealand dollar;
- basket currencies: USD, JPY, EUR and GBP (a country's own currency is dropped from its basket);
- minimum regime length of 26 weeks and at most 10 breaks, with the number of breaks chosen by BIC.

Every country page lets you download the exact R script and input data used, so each result can be reproduced. Earlier applications of this approach to the role of the renminbi as an anchor currency include @balasubramaniam2011yuan and @balasubramaniam2020.

## Objectives

- Operationalise the framework of @sharma2026 to build a continuously updating website that shows the exchange rate regimes (ERRs) of emerging markets.
- Show the structural break dates of past regimes for an emerging market currency.
- Provide a live monitoring system, based on empirical fluctuation processes (efp), that alerts users when there is a potential regime change [@zeileis2010testing].
- Reveal the weights of the basket currencies over time, using exchange rate regressions.
- Allow charts and datasets to be downloaded directly from the website.
- Implement the framework for all emerging market currencies available in the BIS data [@bisdata].

## Intended outcomes

- A practical website for macro traders, central bankers and other finance professionals whose day-to-day work involves understanding currencies.
- Make the framework of @zeileis2010testing accessible to a wide audience, from students of finance and economics to FX specialists making business decisions in firms.
- Make ERR-related data, such as break dates, $R^2$, residual standard error and basket weights, easily available to other researchers.
- A "living" website that updates on its own, without human intervention, and stays available to anyone interested.
